claim: The Arabidopsis thaliana reference genome sequence (TAIR 10) is 125 Mb long.
source: The reference genome sequence of A.thaliana is 125 Mb long (TAIR 10) and contains ~32000, mostly degenerate TE copies that belong to 326 distinct families (Arabidopsis Genome Initiative, 2000; Ahmed et al., 2011).
evidence: Direct statement in the manuscript text citing published references

claim: The Arabidopsis thaliana reference genome contains approximately 32,000 mostly degenerate TE copies.
source: The reference genome sequence of A.thaliana is 125 Mb long (TAIR 10) and contains ~32000, mostly degenerate TE copies that belong to 326 distinct families (Arabidopsis Genome Initiative, 2000; Ahmed et al., 2011).
evidence: Direct statement citing published references

claim: The Arabidopsis thaliana reference genome contains TE copies belonging to 326 distinct families.
source: The reference genome sequence of A.thaliana is 125 Mb long (TAIR 10) and contains ~32000, mostly degenerate TE copies that belong to 326 distinct families (Arabidopsis Genome Initiative, 2000; Ahmed et al., 2011).
evidence: Direct statement citing published references

claim: Transposition activity has been documented experimentally for nine TE families in Arabidopsis thaliana.
source: So far, transposition activity has been documented experimentally for nine TE families, mainly on the basis of studies carried out in the reference accession Col-0 (Ito and Kakutani, 2014; Tsay et al., 1993).
evidence: Direct statement citing published studies

claim: CNVs were detected for 263 TE families in the analysis of 211 Arabidopsis thaliana accessions.
source: CNVs were detected for 263 TE families (Figure 1A and B; Figure 1—source data 1; see 'Materials and methods'), in keeping with the results of a previous study indicating that the vast majority of the TE sequences annotated in the Col-0 reference genome are absent from that of at least one of 80 accessions analyzed (Cao et al., 2011).
evidence: Statement supported by data shown in figures and citing previous study

claim: Non-reference TE insertions with TSDs were identified for 131 TE families in total.
source: Following this approach, non-reference TE insertions with TSDs were identified for 131 TE families in total (Figure 1—source data 2), which all also show CNV (Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: Statement supported by data in source data files

claim: Most (86%) non-reference TE insertions with TSDs are private or shared only by a few accessions.
source: Most (86%) non-reference TE insertions with TSDs are private or shared only by a few accessions and thus they typically correspond to recently derived alleles, as expected (Figure 1E).
evidence: Statement supported by data shown in Figure 1E

claim: Recent transposition activity is detected for between four and 66 TE families in any given accession.
source: Moreover, recent transposition activity is only detected for between four and 66 TE families in any given accession, thus indicating large variations in the composition of the mobilome among accessions (Figure 1F).
evidence: Statement supported by data shown in Figure 1F

claim: The 53 class I COPIA families and the 40 class II Mutator-like (MuDR) families are the most mobile TE families.
source: The 53 class I COPIA families and the 40 class II Mutator-like (MuDR) families are the most mobile, as they account for 1408 and 729 of the 2835 non-reference TE insertions with TSDs identified in total, respectively (Figure 1H and Figure 1—source data 2 and 3).
evidence: Statement supported by data shown in figures and source data files

claim: COPIA families account for 1408 of the 2835 non-reference TE insertions with TSDs identified in total.
source: The 53 class I COPIA families and the 40 class II Mutator-like (MuDR) families are the most mobile, as they account for 1408 and 729 of the 2835 non-reference TE insertions with TSDs identified in total, respectively (Figure 1H and Figure 1—source data 2 and 3).
evidence: Statement supported by data shown in figures and source data files

claim: MuDR families account for 729 of the 2835 non-reference TE insertions with TSDs identified in total.
source: The 53 class I COPIA families and the 40 class II Mutator-like (MuDR) families are the most mobile, as they account for 1408 and 729 of the 2835 non-reference TE insertions with TSDs identified in total, respectively (Figure 1H and Figure 1—source data 2 and 3).
evidence: Statement supported by data shown in figures and source data files

claim: The split-reads approach has a false negative rate of 45% and a false positive rate of 10%.
source: These results indicate therefore that the split-reads approach has a low sensitivity (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C; 45% false negatives and 10% false positives; False Discovery Rate: 15.3%).
evidence: Statement supported by validation analysis shown in supplementary figure

claim: The split-reads approach has a False Discovery Rate of 15.3%.
source: These results indicate therefore that the split-reads approach has a low sensitivity (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C; 45% false negatives and 10% false positives; False Discovery Rate: 15.3%).
evidence: Statement supported by validation analysis shown in supplementary figure

claim: TE-capture validated 87% of the non-reference TE insertions with TSDs that were detected by the split-reads approach.
source: Using genomic DNA extracted from 12 randomly chosen accessions (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D), we could validate by TE-capture most (87%) of the non-reference TE insertions with TSDs that were detected by the split-reads approach (Figure 1—figure supplement 2F; see 'Materials and methods').
evidence: Statement supported by TE-capture validation data shown in supplementary figure

claim: There are at least 165 TE families with recent transposition activity at the species level in Arabidopsis thaliana.
source: Thus, there are altogether at least 165 TE families with recent transposition activity at the species level.
evidence: Statement based on combined results from split-read and TE-capture analyses

claim: Any two Arabidopsis thaliana accessions have accumulated between approximately 200 and 300 newly transposed TE copies since they diverged from each other.
source: Moreover, based on the TE-capture data, we can estimate that since they diverged from each other any two accessions have accumulated between ~200 and ~300 newly transposed TE copies (Figure 1—figure supplement 2H).
evidence: Estimate based on TE-capture data shown in supplementary figure

claim: Copy number correlates positively with the number of TE insertions with TSDs detected by TE-capture.
source: To try to identify such factors, we first established that copy number (CN) correlates positively with the number of TE insertions with TSDs that are detected by TE-capture (Figure 2—figure supplement 1; see 'Materials and methods').
evidence: Statement supported by correlation analysis shown in supplementary figure

claim: Robust correlations with copy number were uncovered for 15 class I and class II TE families when considering thirteen geo-climatic variables.
source: Controlling for population stratification and considering thirteen geo-climatic variables (Hancock et al., 2011), we uncovered robust correlations with CN for 15 class I and class II TE families.
evidence: Statement based on statistical analysis of geo-climatic variables and copy number

claim: ATCOPIA2 and ATCOPIA78 share the highest number of geo-climatic variables correlated with copy number.
source: Among these, ATCOPIA2 and ATCOPIA78 share the highest number of geo-climatic variables correlated with CN (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Statement supported by data shown in supplementary figure

claim: The strongest correlation is between temperature annual range and copy number for ATCOPIA78.
source: Moreover, the strongest correlation is between temperature annual range and CN for ATCOPIA78 (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: Statement supported by data shown in Figure 2A and B

claim: At least one member of the ATCOPIA78 TE family is transcriptionally induced by heat shock in the Col-0 accession.
source: Given that at least one member of this TE family is transcriptionally induced by heat shock in the Col-0 accession (Ito et al., 2011; Cavrak et al., 2014), ATCOPIA78 provides a compelling case of a causal link between climate and TE mobilization.
evidence: Statement citing published studies

claim: ATCOPIA78 provides a compelling case of a causal link between climate and TE mobilization.
source: Given that at least one member of this TE family is transcriptionally induced by heat shock in the Col-0 accession (Ito et al., 2011; Cavrak et al., 2014), ATCOPIA78 provides a compelling case of a causal link between climate and TE mobilization.
evidence: Inference based on correlation data and published studies on heat shock induction

claim: For 33 TE families, a disproportionately large number of SNPs are associated with CNV, preventing further analysis.
source: For 33 TE families, a disproportionately large number of SNPs are associated with CNV, preventing further analysis.
evidence: Statement based on GWAS analysis results

claim: For the remaining 80 TE families, SNPs in linkage disequilibrium with each other and associated with CNVs delineate 230 loci.
source: For the remaining 80 TE families, SNPs in linkage disequilibrium with each other and associated with CNVs delineate 230 loci.
evidence: Statement based on GWAS analysis results

claim: 34% of GWAS loci identified in worldwide accessions are also identified by GWAS using whole genome sequencing data from 180 Swedish accessions.
source: Moreover, 34% of these loci are also identified by GWAS using whole genome sequencing data obtained for another 180 accessions taken from Sweden (Long et al., 2013) (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: Statement based on overlap analysis of GWAS results shown in supplementary figure

claim: Depending on the TE family, GWASs identified from 0 to 33 loci.
source: Depending on the TE family, GWASs identified from 0 to 33 loci and collectively, associations explain between 2% and 67% of the variance in CN (Figure 2C).
evidence: Statement based on GWAS results shown in Figure 2C

claim: GWAS associations collectively explain between 2% and 67% of the variance in copy number.
source: Depending on the TE family, GWASs identified from 0 to 33 loci and collectively, associations explain between 2% and 67% of the variance in CN (Figure 2C).
evidence: Statement based on GWAS results shown in Figure 2C

claim: Among the 334 loci detected in total by GWAS, 130 encompass sites with reference or non-reference TE insertions.
source: Among the 334 loci detected in total, 130 encompass sites with reference or non-reference TE insertions (Figure 2C and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Statement based on GWAS results shown in Figure 2C and supplementary file

claim: Each cis genetic variant explains on average 5.2% of the total variance in copy number.
source: Furthermore, each of these local (cis) genetic variants explains on average 5.2% of the total variance compared with 2.2% for distal (trans) genetic variants.
evidence: Statement based on variance analysis of GWAS results

claim: Each trans genetic variant explains on average 2.2% of the total variance in copy number.
source: Furthermore, each of these local (cis) genetic variants explains on average 5.2% of the total variance compared with 2.2% for distal (trans) genetic variants.
evidence: Statement based on variance analysis of GWAS results

claim: The proportion of copy number variance associated with trans loci is higher for non-autonomous than autonomous class II TE families.
source: Consistent with this possibility, the proportion of CN variance associated with trans loci as well as the number of TE annotations overlapping trans loci are higher for non-autonomous than autonomous class II TE families (Figure 2—figure supplement 3E).
evidence: Statement supported by data shown in supplementary figure

claim: 22 trans loci show association with CNV for two or more TE families.
source: Nonetheless, 22 trans loci stand out as they show association with CNV for two or more TE families (Figure 2D) and a causal link is evident in two cases.
evidence: Statement based on GWAS results shown in Figure 2D

claim: The locus associated with CNV for ATGP2 and ATENSPM2 encodes the transcription factor ARF23.
source: Indeed, the locus associated with CNV for respectively the retrotransposon and DNA transposon families ATGP2 and ATENSPM2 encodes the transcription factor ARF23, which recognizes motifs that are overrepresented in the sequence of these TEs.
evidence: Statement based on GWAS results and sequence analysis

claim: ARF23 recognizes motifs that are overrepresented in the sequence of ATGP2 and ATENSPM2 TEs.
source: Indeed, the locus associated with CNV for respectively the retrotransposon and DNA transposon families ATGP2 and ATENSPM2 encodes the transcription factor ARF23, which recognizes motifs that are overrepresented in the sequence of these TEs.
evidence: Statement based on sequence analysis

claim: The MET2a locus is associated with CNV for four class I and three class II TE families.
source: The second locus is associated with CNV for the largest number of TE families (four class I and three class II families, Figure 2E) and encodes the MET2a protein, a poorly characterized homolog of the main DNA maintenance methyltransferase MET1.
evidence: Statement based on GWAS results shown in Figure 2E

claim: MET2a is a poorly characterized homolog of the main DNA maintenance methyltransferase MET1.
source: The second locus is associated with CNV for the largest number of TE families (four class I and three class II families, Figure 2E) and encodes the MET2a protein, a poorly characterized homolog of the main DNA maintenance methyltransferase MET1.
evidence: Statement based on protein homology

claim: One of the MET2a SNPs leads to a non-synonymous amino-acid substitution (G519E) in a conserved domain of the protein.
source: Moreover, one of the MET2a SNPs is presumably causal as it leads to a non-synonymous amino-acid substitution (G519E) in a conserved domain of the protein (Figure 2F) that in the mammalian homolog Dnmt1 is required for the targeting to replication foci (Klein et al., 2011).
evidence: Statement based on sequence analysis shown in Figure 2F

claim: The conserved domain containing the G519E substitution in MET2a is required for targeting to replication foci in the mammalian homolog Dnmt1.
source: Moreover, one of the MET2a SNPs is presumably causal as it leads to a non-synonymous amino-acid substitution (G519E) in a conserved domain of the protein (Figure 2F) that in the mammalian homolog Dnmt1 is required for the targeting to replication foci (Klein et al., 2011).
evidence: Statement citing published study on Dnmt1

claim: met2a mutant plants lose some DNA methylation exclusively over mobile TE families.
source: A role for MET2a is also supported by the observation that met2a mutant plants (Stroud et al., 2013) lose some DNA methylation exclusively over mobile TE families.
evidence: Statement based on analysis of published methylome data

claim: Loss of DNA methylation in met2a mutant is more pronounced when only considering the seven TE families that show a MET2a association.
source: Furthermore, loss of methylation is more pronounced when only considering the seven TE families that show a MET2a association (Figure 2G).
evidence: Statement based on methylation analysis shown in Figure 2G

claim: CHG sites are the most affected in the met2a mutant.
source: Intriguingly, CHG sites (where H=A, T or C), which are poor substrates for MET1 or Dnmt1 compared to CG sites (Law and Jacobsen, 2010), are the most affected in the met2a mutant.
evidence: Statement based on methylation analysis and citing published knowledge

claim: CHG sites are poor substrates for MET1 or Dnmt1 compared to CG sites.
source: Intriguingly, CHG sites (where H=A, T or C), which are poor substrates for MET1 or Dnmt1 compared to CG sites (Law and Jacobsen, 2010), are the most affected in the met2a mutant.
evidence: Statement citing published knowledge

claim: Non-reference TE insertions with TSDs are distributed almost evenly along chromosomes.
source: To distinguish between these possibilities, we looked at the genomic location of the 2835 non-reference TE insertions with TSDs detected with the split-reads approach and found that they are distributed almost evenly along chromosomes (Figure 3A).
evidence: Statement based on genomic distribution analysis shown in Figure 3A

claim: There is a clear trend towards a more pericentromeric localization when only considering non-reference TE insertions with TSDs that are shared by two or more accessions.
source: However, there is a clear trend towards a more pericentromeric localization when only considering non-reference TE insertions with TSDs that are shared by two or more accessions and that are thus presumably more ancestral (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Statement based on genomic distribution analysis shown in figures

claim: The density of non-reference TE insertions with TSDs positively correlates with the recombination rate.
source: Moreover, the density of non-reference TE insertions with TSDs positively correlates with the recombination rate but negatively with gene density (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, D and E).
evidence: Statement based on correlation analysis shown in supplementary figures

claim: The density of non-reference TE insertions with TSDs negatively correlates with gene density.
source: Moreover, the density of non-reference TE insertions with TSDs positively correlates with the recombination rate but negatively with gene density (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, D and E).
evidence: Statement based on correlation analysis shown in supplementary figures

claim: Except for COPIA families, non-reference TE insertions with TSDs are globally under-represented within genes.
source: Finally, except for COPIA families, non-reference TE insertions with TSDs are globally under-represented within genes, where they are expected to be most detrimental (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1F and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Statement based on distribution analysis shown in figures

claim: TEs insert equally throughout the genome and are preferentially purged over time from the chromosome arms because of their deleterious effects on adjacent genes.
source: Collectively, these observations provide strong evidence that TEs insert equally throughout the genome and are preferentially purged over time from the chromosome arms because of their deleterious effects on adjacent genes rather than as a consequence of ectopic homologous recombination.
evidence: Inference based on multiple lines of evidence including distribution patterns and correlation analyses

claim: Private non-reference COPIA insertions with TSDs are enriched at coding sequences.
source: In agreement with previous observations (Fu et al., 2013; Miyao et al., 2003), private non-reference COPIA and MuDR insertions with TSDs are enriched at coding sequences and transcriptional start sites (TSS), respectively (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Statement based on metagene analysis shown in supplementary figure and citing previous studies

claim: Private non-reference MuDR insertions with TSDs are enriched at transcriptional start sites (TSS).
source: In agreement with previous observations (Fu et al., 2013; Miyao et al., 2003), private non-reference COPIA and MuDR insertions with TSDs are enriched at coding sequences and transcriptional start sites (TSS), respectively (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Statement based on metagene analysis shown in supplementary figure and citing previous studies

claim: LINEs tend to insert within poly(A) tracks.
source: For example, LINEs tend to insert within poly(A) tracks, as expected for this superfamily of non-LTR retrotransposons, which integrate into the genome via poly(A)-dependent, target site–primed reverse transcription (TPRT; Beck et al., 2011).
evidence: Statement based on sequence motif analysis and citing published knowledge

claim: For a large fraction of genes, expression is significantly altered when TEs insert within or near them.
source: Comparison of the distribution of the observed and expected expression ratios indicates that for a large fraction of genes, expression is indeed significantly altered when TEs insert within or near them (Figure 3D, p<1.9×10-5).
evidence: Statement based on transcriptome analysis shown in Figure 3D with statistical significance

claim: Expression alterations caused by TE insertions are most pronounced for COPIA insertions.
source: These alterations are most pronounced for the COPIA insertions, which are overrepresented in genes and less pronounced for the MuDR insertions, despite the latter being overrepresented around the TSS of genes (Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Statement based on transcriptome analysis shown in figures

claim: Expression alterations caused by TE insertions are less pronounced for MuDR insertions.
source: These alterations are most pronounced for the COPIA insertions, which are overrepresented in genes and less pronounced for the MuDR insertions, despite the latter being overrepresented around the TSS of genes (Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Statement based on transcriptome analysis shown in figures

claim: TE insertions induce both increases and decreases in gene expression with equal frequency.
source: This notwithstanding, it is clear that TE insertions induce both increases and decreases in gene expression with equal frequency (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: Statement based on transcriptome analysis shown in figures

claim: COPIA insertions have more dramatic and systematic effects on gene expression in stressed plants.
source: COPIA insertions were found to have more dramatic and systematic effects on gene expression in stressed plants (Figure 3—figure supplement 4) which in the case of ATCOPIA78 can be related to its transcriptional sensitivity to heat shock (Ito et al., 2011; Cavrak et al., 2014).
evidence: Statement based on RT-qPCR analysis shown in supplementary figure and citing published studies

claim: Mobile TE families have on average higher CG, CHG and CHH methylation than non-mobile TE families.
source: Analysis of this data set first indicated that mobile TE families have on average higher CG, CHG and CHH methylation than non-mobile TE families (Figure 4A).
evidence: Statement based on methylome analysis shown in Figure 4A

claim: DNA methylation is higher for most mobile TE families in the accessions with evidence of recent transposition activity.
source: Furthermore, DNA methylation is also higher for most mobile TE families in the accessions with evidence of recent transposition activity (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Statement based on methylome analysis shown in supplementary figure

claim: Mobile TE families suffer less sporadic DNA methylation loss than non-mobile families.
source: Mobile TE families suffer less sporadic DNA methylation loss than non-mobile families (Figure 4B).
evidence: Statement based on analysis of mutation accumulation lines shown in Figure 4B

claim: Approximately 10% of TE insertion sites are methylated in most accessions, including systematically in the one(s) containing the TE.
source: Approximately 10% of sites are methylated in most accessions, including systematically in the one(s) containing the TE.
evidence: Statement based on methylome analysis of insertion sites

claim: 40% of TE insertion sites are devoid of methylation in the accession(s) containing the TE insertion as well as in most of the other accessions.
source: In contrast, another 40% of sites are devoid of methylation in the accession(s) containing the TE insertion as well as in most of the other accessions.
evidence: Statement based on methylome analysis of insertion sites

claim: 50% of TE insertion sites are methylated exclusively or almost exclusively in the accession(s) with the TE insertion.
source: Finally, 50% of sites are methylated exclusively or almost exclusively in the accession(s) with the TE insertion (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), thus suggesting that at these sites TEs are methylated and that DNA methylation did spread into adjacent sequences.
evidence: Statement based on methylome analysis shown in supplementary figure

claim: DNA methylation associated with TE insertions generally extends for up to 300 bp on both sides of the insertions.
source: Further analysis of DNA methylation associated with TE insertions indicates that it affects all three sequence contexts and that it generally extends for up to 300 bp on both sides of the insertions (Figure 4D and E; Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), a distance that closely matches that previously reported for the spreading of DNA methylation from RdDM targets (Ahmed et al., 2011).
evidence: Statement based on methylome analysis shown in figures and citing previous study

claim: For 243 insertion sites, DNA methylation extends over much longer distances (up to 3.5 kb) on one or the other side of the insertion.
source: For 243 insertion sites however, DNA methylation extends over much longer distances (up to 3.5 kb) on one or the other side of the insertion (Figure 4D and E).
evidence: Statement based on methylome analysis shown in figures

claim: Long-distance DNA methylation aligns with 24-nt siRNAs.
source: In addition, analysis of Col-0 small RNA-seq data (Fahlgren et al., 2009) indicates that in contrast to short-distance DNA methylation, long-distance DNA methylation aligns with 24-nt siRNAs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Statement based on small RNA-seq analysis shown in supplementary figure and citing published data

claim: Genes affected by long-distance DNA methylation tend to be most highly expressed in both pollen and seeds in Col-0.
source: Moreover, genes affected by long-distance DNA methylation in accessions other than Col-0 tend in the latter accession, where they are by definition in the ancestral state, to be most highly expressed in both pollen and seeds and more highly expressed in these two organs than genes affected by short-distance DNA methylation (Figure 4G).
evidence: Statement based on expression analysis shown in Figure 4G

claim: TE-associated DNA methylation accounts for at least 7% of the gene C-DMRs identified in nature.
source: Finally, our analysis of TE-associated DNA methylation indicates that it accounts for at least 7% of the so-called gene C-DMRs (i.e. regions of differential methylation at CG, CHG and CHH sites) identified in nature, which are typically low frequency gain of DNA methylation variants (Schmitz et al., 2013).
evidence: Statement based on analysis of TE-associated methylation and citing published study

claim: Nineteen 10 kb windows were detected with a high load of non-reference TE insertions.
source: Although TEs tend to insert with no overt bias at the genome scale (Figure 3A), we detected nineteen 10 kb windows with a high load of non-reference TE insertions (Figure 5A).
evidence: Statement based on genomic distribution analysis shown in Figure 5A

claim: Three of the 10 kb windows with high TE insertion load span genes encoding nucleotide-binding domain and leucine-rich repeat containing (NLR) proteins.
source: In fact, three of these 10 kb windows span genes encoding nucleotide-binding domain and leucine-rich repeat containing (NLR) proteins, which function as immune receptors in plants and are known to be under diversifying selection (Chae et al., 2014).
evidence: Statement based on genomic analysis and citing published knowledge

claim: NLR proteins function as immune receptors in plants and are known to be under diversifying selection.
source: In fact, three of these 10 kb windows span genes encoding nucleotide-binding domain and leucine-rich repeat containing (NLR) proteins, which function as immune receptors in plants and are known to be under diversifying selection (Chae et al., 2014).
evidence: Statement citing published knowledge

claim: The FLC locus has the highest number of non-reference TE insertions (seven in total) across the genome.
source: Remarkably, the FLC locus has the highest number of non-reference TE insertions (seven in total) across the genome.
evidence: Statement based on genomic distribution analysis

claim: The seven FLC TE insertions belong to several COPIA families and affect four distinct FLC haplotypes in total.
source: These insertions belong to several COPIA families and affect four distinct FLC haplotypes in total (Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Statement based on haplotype analysis shown in figures

claim: Five FLC TE insertions are located within the first intron.
source: Moreover, five insertions are located within the first intron (Figure 5B), which plays an important role in the epigenetic regulation of FLC in response to cold (Ietswaart et al., 2012).
evidence: Statement based on genomic location analysis shown in Figure 5B and citing published study

claim: The first intron of FLC plays an important role in the epigenetic regulation of FLC in response to cold.
source: Moreover, five insertions are located within the first intron (Figure 5B), which plays an important role in the epigenetic regulation of FLC in response to cold (Ietswaart et al., 2012).
evidence: Statement citing published study

claim: TE-containing accessions have systematically much reduced FLC expression compared to their TE-free counterparts.
source: Results of these comparisons indicate that the TE-containing accessions have systematically much reduced FLC expression and flower much earlier than their TE-free counterparts (Figure 5C and D; Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: Statement based on expression and phenotype analysis shown in figures

claim: TE-containing accessions flower much earlier than their TE-free counterparts.
source: Results of these comparisons indicate that the TE-containing accessions have systematically much reduced FLC expression and flower much earlier than their TE-free counterparts (Figure 5C and D; Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: Statement based on phenotype analysis shown in figures

claim: TEs are recurrent generators of major effect FLC alleles.
source: Thus, we can conclude that TEs are recurrent generators of major effect FLC alleles, which in turn suggests that they contribute significantly to the high level of allelic heterogeneity observed at this locus (Li et al., 2014)
evidence: Inference based on expression and phenotype data and citing published study

claim: The A. thaliana mobilome is composed of at least half of the 326 TE families annotated in the reference genome.
source: We have shown that the A. thaliana mobilome is particularly rich at the species level, being composed of at least half of the 326 TE families that are annotated in the reference genome.
evidence: Summary statement based on the study's findings

claim: Most TE families are mere molecular fossils in A. thaliana according to the prevailing view.
source: This finding is at odds with the prevailing view that most TE families are mere molecular fossils in A. thaliana, since they contain a much lower proportion of 'young', i.e. non-degenerated TE copies than in the close relative A. lyrata (Hu et al., 2011; Maumus and Quesneville, 2014).
evidence: Statement describing prevailing view and citing published studies

claim: A. thaliana contains a much lower proportion of 'young' TE copies than A. lyrata.
source: This finding is at odds with the prevailing view that most TE families are mere molecular fossils in A. thaliana, since they contain a much lower proportion of 'young', i.e. non-degenerated TE copies than in the close relative A. lyrata (Hu et al., 2011; Maumus and Quesneville, 2014).
evidence: Statement citing published studies

claim: A. thaliana is predominantly self-fertilizing.
source: Furthermore, because A. thaliana is predominantly self-fertilizing, the purging of deleterious TE insertions should be accelerated in this species compared to A. lyrata, which is an obligated out-crosser.
evidence: Statement based on established knowledge about A. thaliana mating system

claim: A. lyrata is an obligated out-crosser.
source: Furthermore, because A. thaliana is predominantly self-fertilizing, the purging of deleterious TE insertions should be accelerated in this species compared to A. lyrata, which is an obligated out-crosser.
evidence: Statement based on established knowledge about A. lyrata mating system

claim: The purging of deleterious TE insertions should be accelerated in A. thaliana compared to A. lyrata.
source: Furthermore, because A. thaliana is predominantly self-fertilizing, the purging of deleterious TE insertions should be accelerated in this species compared to A. lyrata, which is an obligated out-crosser.
evidence: Inference based on differences in mating systems

claim: The composition and activity of the mobilome vary greatly between accessions.
source: We have also shown that the composition and activity of the mobilome vary greatly between accessions.
evidence: Summary statement based on the study's findings

claim: TE families contain only one or a few active, autonomous (i.e. master) TE copies at any one time.
source: GWASs revealed that this variation is caused in part by sequence polymorphisms within the TEs themselves (cis variation), which is in agreement with empirical data and theoretical models indicating that TE families contain only one or a few active, autonomous (i.e. master) TE copies at any one time (Becker et al., 2011).
evidence: Statement citing published empirical data and theoretical models

claim: Natural variation at the MET2a locus has a significant impact on mobilome composition and activity across accessions.
source: Another important result of the GWASs is that natural variation at the MET2a locus, which encodes a poorly characterized DNA methyltransferase, has a significant impact on mobilome composition and activity across accessions, being associated with differential transposition activity for seven class I and class II TE families.
evidence: Summary statement based on GWAS results

claim: Temperature annual range is a clear contributor to the variation in ATCOPIA78 mobilization across accessions.
source: Being a complex trait, TE mobilization is also modulated by environmental factors, and we have identified temperature annual range as a clear contributor to the variation in ATCOPIA78 mobilization across accessions.
evidence: Summary statement based on climate correlation analysis

claim: ATCOPIA78 may endow A. thaliana with a unique ability to adapt to global warming by facilitating the creation of early flowering FLC alleles.
source: It is therefore tempting to speculate that ATCOPIA78 may endow A. thaliana with a unique ability to adapt to global warming and the associated increase in droughts by facilitating the creation of early flowering FLC alleles.
evidence: Speculative statement based on the study's findings

claim: Part of the missing heritability in GWASs may be accounted for by recent and rare TE insertion alleles with large effects.
source: In summary, our findings have far reaching implications, as they indicate that part of the missing heritability that plagues many GWASs may be accounted for by recent and thus rare TE insertion alleles with large effects (Vinkhuyzen et al., 2013; Brachi et al., 2011).
evidence: Inference based on the study's findings and citing published studies on missing heritability

claim: Transposable elements are classified as retrotransposons (class I) or DNA transposons (class II) depending on whether their mobilization relies on a RNA or DNA intermediate.
source: Depending on whether their mobilization relies on a RNA or DNA intermediate, they are classified as retrotransposons (class I) or DNA transposons (class II), respectively (Slotkin and Martienssen, 2007).
evidence: Statement citing published classification system

claim: TEs can disrupt genes through insertion and also through excision in the case of DNA transposons.
source: In particular, TEs can disrupt genes through insertion and also through excision in the case of DNA transposons.
evidence: Statement based on established knowledge about TE mechanisms

claim: TE mobilization is a source of both germline and somatic mutations.
source: Thus, TE mobilization is a source of both germline and somatic mutations (Richardson et al., 2015; Barrón et al., 2014; Lisch, 2013).
